To start the pg_cron background worker, you need to add pg_cron to `shared_preload_libraries` in postgresql.conf. Note that pg_cron does not run any jobs as a long a server is in hot standby mode, but it automatically starts when the server is promoted.
**Important**: By default, pg_cron uses libpq to open a new connection to the local database, which needs to be allowed by pg_hba.conf.

It may be necessary to enable `trust` authentication for connections coming from localhost in for the user running the cron job, or you can add the password to a .pgpass file, which libpq will use when opening a connection.
You can also use a unix domain socket directory as the hostname and enable `trust` authentication for local connections in pg_hba.conf, which is normally safe:

- **Patterns** — `normalizeQuery()` rollup with cumulative cost (Runs / Avg dur / **Total dur** / Max mem / Read rows / Read bytes), default sort Total dur DESC — finds the patterns hogging the most wall-clock time across all repetitions
- **By table** — `arrayJoin(tables)` per-table rollup with `arrayFilter` push-down so busy clusters return in ~1 s

- **Histogram** — distribution of duration / memory / read rows / read bytes across the active window, with **p50 / p95 / p99** chips (p99 amber-tinted to flag the tail)
- **Memory** — server RAM breakdown (RSS attributed to active queries / caches / merges / primary keys / index, vs total), allocator history, and a top-memory-queries table
- **CPU** — load avg / threads / pools, CPU mode-split + concurrency charts, and a top-CPU-queries table

SpiderNode is a full-stack, production-ready uptime monitoring SaaS designed for modern engineering teams and independent developers. Monitor HTTP/HTTPS endpoints, capture real-time latency metrics, orchestrate automated incident responses, and dispatch instant Telegram alerts — all backed by an intelligent in-memory write-batching engine designed to drastically minimize database compute.
Key Features • System Architecture • Tech Stack • Quick Start • Cron & Polling Engine • Deployment • API Reference
- High-precision latency profiling (`performance.now()`), response status code tracking (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx), and automatic HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect traversal.
- Fail-safe 10-second request timeout controller (`AbortController`) to eliminate zombie worker threads.
- Up to **~93% reduction in database write compute** by buffering routine `UP` state checks in an in-memory queue (`db-batcher.ts`) and flushing to PostgreSQL in bulk every 15 minutes.
- **Immediate Low-Latency Slow Path**: State transitions (`UP ⇄ DOWN` or first ping) bypass the memory buffer and commit immediately to the database to ensure zero incident-delay.
- Graceful process termination handlers (`SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`) guarantee that buffered memory snapshots are flushed prior to shutdown.
- Automatically provisions an `ONGOING` incident with detailed diagnostic metadata (status code, timeout message, timestamp) upon downtime.
- Automatically transitions incidents to `RESOLVED` when the target endpoint recovers.
- Zero-friction bot linking using deep-link start parameters (`/start <userId>`).

`setup` registers the MCP server (`claude mcp add -s user linksee -- npx -y linksee-memory`), installs the agent skill, adds a `Stop` hook that saves each session, and wires the re-injection guard for every repo (`--project-guard` for this repo only, `--no-guard` to skip). Running it again changes nothing that is already in place.
|`~/.claude.json`|the `linksee` MCP server (via `claude mcp add`) — undo with `claude mcp remove linksee`|

|`~/.claude/settings.json`|the `Stop` hook (auto-capture) and the `SessionStart` / `PreToolUse` guard hooks. Merged into what is there — other hooks and settings are kept. If the file does not parse, setup leaves it untouched and says so. Before changing it, setup keeps the previous file as `settings.json.bak-<timestamp>`: to undo, copy that file back over `settings.json`.|

|`~/.linksee-memory/runtime/<version>/`|only when setup ran from a temporary location (`npx`, `pnpm dlx`, `bunx`, or the system temp directory): setup runs `npm install --prefix ~/.linksee-memory/runtime/<version> --no-save --omit=dev linksee-memory@<version>` once (shown with its size; this downloads from the npm registry), because the hooks call `node` on it directly and those locations are temporary. Older versions are not removed automatically (about 35 MB each): setup prints the folder, and `npx -y linksee-memory runtime prune` lists them with what references each. With `--yes --scope-confirmed` it deletes only versions no settings file references; it cannot see other repos where you ran `setup --project` (pass their `.claude/settings.json` with `--settings`), and if a settings file cannot be read or parsed it deletes nothing. If the install fails, the hooks stay on the npx form.|
|`~/.linksee-memory/telemetry-consent`|your telemetry answer (`off` unless you said yes)|

To remove everything: `claude mcp remove linksee`, delete the linksee hooks from `settings.json` (or copy the `.bak` back), then `rm -rf ~/.claude/skills/linksee-memory ~/.linksee-memory` — the last one deletes the memory stored in that folder. It does not reach copies you made yourself (for example to hand the memory over) or telemetry already sent if you opted in. Linksee itself never sends memory text anywhere. - **Contradiction warned or blocked (Claude Code only):** the guard can only tell that an edit contradicts a decision if you give it the strings that mean "contradiction": `anchor: { violation_signal: ["pgvector"] }`. An empty `anchor: {}` is stored as a constraint and is re-injected, never matched as a contradiction. A match warns; after `resolve_drift(action: "harden")` it blocks. The guard fails open: its own errors never block anything. Details: docs/guard.md.

- **Telemetry is opt-in and OFF by default.** `setup` asks once; nothing is sent unless you agree there (or set `LINKSEE_TELEMETRY=basic`). Even then it never sends your source code, file contents, prompts, conversation, entity/project names, or the memory DB — only anonymous counters (details).
- **`share_draft` makes a link only; Linksee itself never sends it.** The user opens it and decides (details).

- **Hooks are documented and removable.** `setup` adds a Stop hook (session capture) and the guard hooks (skip them with `--no-guard`). They send nothing unless you opted in to telemetry (then the Stop hook posts one set of counters per session). Hooks written in the `npx -y` form — the fallback when setup cannot write a direct `node` call — start npm, which checks the registry. They are time-bounded, fail-open (a hook error never breaks your session), and are listed under Uninstall.
